thesis: The Bitcoin Passport Index isn't a neutral ranking—it's a commercial product engineered to make cryptocurrency-friendly jurisdictions look like the best places to live, using methodology that lets a company with financial stakes in crypto adoption grade its own investment thesis.
hook: Imagine ranking the world's best restaurants, but the steakhouse industry gets to design the scorecard—and then buys the top spot.
stakes: If you're making decisions about where to live, work, or invest based on indexes like this, you deserve to know when the chef is also the critic. This isn't just about one ranking; it's about how the entire ecosystem of crypto-adjacent indices shapes your options without disclosing its conflicts.
counterpoint: Even a biased index can surface genuine information—if El Salvador's Bitcoin policies have created real advantages, those deserve scrutiny regardless of who found them.
implication: Before you use any passport index to guide your decisions, ask who funded it, what they sell, and whose interests their methodology quietly protects. The score might be about something other than what it claims to measure.
close: El Salvador landed at number one because a company with skin in the game built a ruler that measures what it wants to sell. Your freedom to move across borders is being scored by people who profit from certain answers. So next time an index tells you where sovereignty lives, find out who's holding the pen before you trust the rankings. The passport that gets you into 131 countries came in first because 45 percent of the vote was Bitcoin-shaped—and that's a recipe written by the guests, not the chefs.
